# Nullable Salesperson Key

**Decision.** Declare `mart.FACT_SALES.SalesPersonID` as `INT NULL` with a foreign key to
`mart.DIM_SALESPERSON`, and load every order line regardless of whether a salesperson exists.

**Date.** 2026-07-25, [[data-warehousing-and-business-intelligence]].

## Why

> "SalesPersonID is nullable: roughly 60% of AdventureWorks orders are online and have no
> salesperson. Requiring one -- or filtering the load to rows that have one -- would discard most of
> the sales the warehouse exists to measure."
> — Data-Warehousing-and-Business-Intelligence/sql/02_star_schema/01_create_star_schema.sql, 2026-07-25

The reasoning is about **grain**, not about nullability. The fact table's grain is one row per sales
order line ([[fact-grain]]), and it is enforced by the primary key. A `NOT NULL` on a dimension key
that the source genuinely does not always have silently redefines that grain to "one row per order
line *that had a salesperson*" — a different table answering a different question, with the majority
of revenue missing. The dimension key is optional because the *relationship* is optional in the
business, and the fact table's job is to record the business.

`ShipDateKey` is nullable in the same DDL for the same class of reason: an unshipped order is a real
order. A nullable foreign key is still enforced by SQL Server when a value *is* present, so the
constraint does no less work — see [[sql-server]].

## The companion rule, in the other direction

The load script draws the opposite line for descriptive dimension attributes:

> "ISNULL, not the column DEFAULT. A DEFAULT applies only when no value is supplied; selecting an
> explicit NULL into the column bypasses it, so the declared 'Unknown' would never take effect."
> — Data-Warehousing-and-Business-Intelligence/sql/02_star_schema/02_load_star_schema.sql, 2026-07-25

Missing *descriptions* — a product with no colour, no subcategory, no category — are replaced with a
literal `'Unknown'` at load time, because a report grouping by colour should show an Unknown bucket
rather than dropping rows. Missing *relationships* stay `NULL`. Two kinds of absence, two
treatments, both written down. See [[etl-load-order]].

## Alternatives rejected

| Option | Why not | Evidenced? |
|---|---|---|
| **`NOT NULL` on the key** | most orders have no salesperson; the load would fail or the rows would be unloadable | yes — named in the DDL comment |
| **Filter the load to rows that have a salesperson** | discards the majority of sales; silently changes the grain | yes — named in the DDL comment |
| **An "Unknown salesperson" member in the dimension, with a sentinel key** | — | **no** |

The third row is the standard Kimball answer to an optional dimension relationship: add a `-1`
"Unknown" row to the dimension so every fact row has a real key and `INNER JOIN` behaves. It would
also have matched the `'Unknown'` treatment the same repo uses for descriptive attributes, above.

**TODO:** nothing in the repo names the sentinel-member option, so there is no record of it being
considered and rejected. Do not read its absence as a decision. `confidence: low` on that sub-claim.

## The number is an assertion

**TODO:** "roughly 60% of AdventureWorks orders are online" appears in three places in the repository
and all three are the same uncomputed statement — no query, no output, no committed result backs it.
The same applies to a nearby claim about the count of products with a zero list price. Whether either
was measured or recalled is unknown; `confidence: low` on both figures. The decision does not depend
on the exact share — "most" is enough to carry it — but the number should not be cited from here as
though it were measured. This is the class of claim [[verify-the-load-dont-declare-it]] exists to
turn into a query, and in this repo the queries are written but never run and recorded.

Page `confidence: medium`: the rationale is verbatim in the DDL and carried through independently by
the load script, which joins header to detail with no salesperson filter — but it is one deliverable
by one author and was not covered in the interview.
